Ticket Status Notification

Ticket Information

Ticket Number: 2025112000296

Ticket Location: 5908 W THUNDERBIRD RD
GLENDALE, MARICOPA, AZ United States
33.6112259214948, -112.186424606631 

Due Date: 11/24/2025 7:00 PM ET

Company: CHRISTY SIGNS

Phone: 6022424488

Fax/Email:  / STEVE@CHRISTYSIGNS.COM

 




Reason for Notification

Notification Type: Bore Standby        Date: 11/20/2025

You have indicated on the Locate Request(s) that you intend to use Boring in your work area. To ensure the integrity of our system, Southwest Gas is requesting you call us prior to exposing our facilities. Southwest Gas requires a representative to be present to verify our facilities prior to boring across or parallel within 5-feet of Southwest Gas facilities. This is to confirm that you have in fact exposed our line and confirm the line depth to assure a safe bore operation by positive identification of our facilities. Call to schedule a standby a minimum of two hours prior to work identified above.

Notify an SWG representative when boring parallel to any Southwest Gas facilities within 5-feet of the bore. This applies to vertical boring as well.

1.	Notify an SWG representative when boring across any Southwest Gas facilities.

2.	Pothole any gas facilities within 24-inches of the proposed bore path.

3.	Hand digging is required within 24-inches of the gas facility markings, and all gas facilities must be identified, protected, and exposed during any boring operations.

4.	Before the excavation, schedule a Bore Standby with a SWG representative to be present to verify the buried facilities and monitor the boring activities.

Please contact your local SWG field office to schedule a Bore Standby with a Southwest Gas representative a

minimum of 2 hours prior.

 602-484-5085

 For more information regarding safe digging practices, please visit swgas.com

Locate Requester will notify its employees and any of their subcontractors of these requirements.

If you have any questions or need any assistance, please notify Southwest Gas immediately.

Southwest Gas Corporation Business Hours (Mon-Fri between 600 a.m. & 2:30 p.m.) After Hours Emergency: 877-860-6020

EXCAVATOR PRECAUTIONARY GUIDELINES

 

This information is to assist excavators in the proper identification of gas facilities, and precautions to be taken when working around gas facilities.  The information provided here is not to be considered all-inclusive. All excavators digging within the vicinity of gas pipelines must protect the pipelines in accordance with the applicable One-Call law. The following are guidelines that will assist you in protecting the public, you, and the gas facilities.

If any gas pipelines are damaged, federal law requires that you call Southwest Gas Corporation (SWG). Additionally, if the damage results in the escape of gas, you must call the Emergency Number 911.  Note: Damage includes damage to steel pipeline coatings, gouges in plastic pipe, damaged tracer wire, dents or scrapes in steel pipe, etc.

Gas pipeline markers are used to alert the public that gas pipelines are buried in the general area. These markers may or may not be placed directly over the gas facility. When performing an excavation within 10’ of a “High Pressure” marked facility, please contact SWG to arrange for stand by personnel to be present.

 

PLASTIC PIPELINES:  Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) pipe is one type of plastic pipe used in the SWG gas distribution system.  PVC may be faint yellow, gray or white in color and range in size from ½" to 2" in diameter.  PVC is not as flexible as the polyethylene (PE) pipe that SWG installs today. The integrity of PVC can be compromised if scratched or subjected to external loads and/or stresses.  PE is another type of plastic pipe used in SWG’s system.  PE may be found in various colors and range in size from ½" to 8" in diameter.  Although PE is a more flexible material, its integrity can be compromised if scratched or nicked.  Many plastic gas pipelines are installed with a tracer wire in order to locate the facility.  If a tracer wire is or has been severed or damaged, call SWG.  We will repair the damaged wire at no charge.

 

STEEL PIPELINES: Steel gas pipelines, used in both SWG gas distribution and high-pressure transmission systems, range in size from ½" to 24" in diameter and are also susceptible to damage.  Dents and gouges in the steel will affect the integrity of the pipe, so precautionary measures must be taken during excavation.  Steel pipelines are protected with an approved coating material that helps prevent deterioration of the pipe and can be found in various colors.  If during excavation the coating is torn or damaged, contact SWG immediately to facilitate the repairs at no charge.  Call us before disturbing any mastic coating on active or abandoned steel pipe.  The coating is likely to contain regulated asbestos fibers that can be harmful to your employees.

 

Typically, most gas pipes have specific identification markings on them or on the coating.  Care should be taken to support and protect all gas pipelines, as required by law, when exposed or crossed during excavation activities.  Additionally, care must be taken while exposing existing facilities as they may or may not have padding and shading surrounding them as outlined below.  If any gas pipeline is damaged, call SWG immediately to facilitate the proper pipeline repairs.  When excavations have been completed, gas pipelines must be properly padded, shaded, and backfilled per SWG standards, as shown in the drawing below.  SWG specifications for padding and shading material call for it to be able to sift through a 3/8" screen and be smooth and relatively rock free.  Excavations must be compacted to meet the requirements of local authorities.  During backfill activities it is very important to compact the soil beneath the gas pipe to properly support it. Also, it is important to avoid mechanically compacting the soil directly over the gas pipe to eliminate any unnecessary external stresses.  Steps must be taken during this process to protect the gas pipeline from excessive external loadings.  If other utilities or substructures are to be installed in the same excavation as a gas pipeline, the proper clearances shown in the drawing must be maintained.

If at any time during excavation activities you smell gas, call SWG and 911.

*	DO NOT attempt to control or stop the flow of natural gas, or make repairs.
*	DO NOT turn on, turn off, or attempt to move or operate equipment near the line break or point of leakage.
*	DO NOT enter the area where the natural gas is escaping.
*	DO NOT allow others to enter the area.
*	DO NOT leave the scene of the incident until assistance has arrived.
*	DO secure the area and prevent others from entering.
*	DO eliminate sources of ignition, such as sparks or flames, near the gaseous atmosphere.

For more information on the types of gas pipe used by SWG, positive identification of gas facilities, or if you have any questions, please contact the SWG office nearest you. Additional information on natural gas safety is included in our Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) located at www.swgas.com/emergencysafety <http://www.swgas.com/emergencysafety> .

Please forward to the appropriate excavator.




Esta información tiene como objetivo ayudar a los excavadores a identificar adecuadamente las instalaciones de gas y a conocer las precauciones que deben tener cuando trabajan cerca de ellas. La información aquí provista no es exhaustiva. Todos los excavadores que trabajen en cercanías de gasoductos deben protegerlos de acuerdo con la ley vigente sobre excavaciones. Las siguientes son pautas que lo ayudarán a proteger al público, a usted mismo y a las instalaciones de gas.

Si el gasoducto está dañado, la ley federal exige que llame a Southwest Gas Corporation (SWG). Además, si el daño causa un escape de gas, debe llamar al número para emergencias 911. Nota: Los daños pueden ser daños en el recubrimiento de las tuberías de acero, aberturas en las tuberías plásticas, daños en el alambre de rastreo, mellas o raspaduras en las tuberías de acero, etc.

 

Se usan señales para advertir al público de que hay gasoductos enterrados en el área. Estas señales pueden ponerse directamente sobre la instalación de gas o no. Cuando se lleva a cabo una excavación dentro de los 10’ de una instalación señalizada como “High Pressure” (de alta presión), comuníquese con SWG para que envíen personal de respaldo.

TUBERÍAS PLÁSTICAS Las tuberías de policloruro de vinilo (PVC) son un tipo de tubería plástica que SWG usa en el sistema de distribución. Las tuberías de PVC pueden ser de color amarillo claro, gris o blanco, y su tamaño puede ir desde ½” hasta 2” de diámetro. Las tuberías de PVC no son tan flexibles como las de polietileno (PE) que SWG instala hoy. El PVC puede arruinarse si se raya o se somete a pesos o tensiones extremos. Las tuberías de PE son otro tipo de tuberías plásticas que SWG usa en su sistema. Las tuberías de PE pueden ser de varios colores, y su tamaño va desde ½” hasta 8” de diámetro. Aunque el PE es un material más flexible, puede arruinarse si se raya o corta. Muchos gasoductos de plástico se instalan con un alambre de rastreo para ubicar la instalación. Si el alambre de rastreo se corta o daña, llame a SWG. Lo repararemos sin cargo.

 

TUBERÍAS DE ACERO Las tuberías de gas de acero, usadas por SWG tanto para la distribución de gas como para los sistemas de transmisión a alta presión, varían en tamaño desde 1/2" hasta 24" de diámetro y también son susceptibles a los daños. Las mellas y aberturas en el acero pueden afectar la integridad de la tubería. Por eso, deben tomarse medidas de precaución durante la excavación. Las tuberías de acero se protegen con un material de recubrimiento aprobado que ayuda a prevenir su deterioro y puede ser de varios colores. Si durante la excavación el recubrimiento se desprende o daña, comuníquese con SWG de inmediato para facilitar las reparaciones sin cargo. Llámenos antes de quitar cualquier recubrimiento de masilla de una tubería de acero activa o abandonada. Es posible que el recubrimiento contenga fibras de amianto reglamentario que pueden ser dañinas para sus empleados.

 

En general, las tuberías de gas tienen marcas de identificación específicas sobre ellas o sobre el recubrimiento. Debe tenerse precaución y sostener y proteger todos los gasoductos, según lo requiera la ley, cuando se expongan o crucen durante la excavación. Además, debe tenerse cuidado al exponer instalaciones existentes, ya que pueden o no, tener relleno a su alrededor, como se detalla más abajo. Si un gasoducto está dañado, llame a SWG de inmediato para facilitar las reparaciones necesarias. Cuando finalicen las excavaciones, los gasoductos deben ser rellenados según las normas de SWG, como se muestra en el dibujo más abajo. Las especificaciones de SWG para el material de relleno indican que este debe poder pasar a través de un tamiz de 3/8”, ser suave y estar relativamente libre de escombros.  Las excavaciones deben ser compactadas para cumplir con los requisitos de las autoridades locales. Durante el rellenado, es muy importante compactar el suelo bajo el gasoducto, a fin de sujetarlo apropiadamente. También es importante evitar compactar mecánicamente el suelo que está sobre el gasoducto para eliminar tensiones externas innecesarias. Deben tomarse medidas durante este proceso para proteger el gasoducto de cargas externas excesivas. Si se deben instalar otros servicios o subestructuras en la misma excavación del gasoducto, deben respetarse las distancias que se muestran en el dibujo.

Si en cualquier momento durante la excavación percibe olor a gas, llame a SWG y al 911.

*	NO intente controlar ni parar el flujo de gas natural ni de hacer reparaciones.
*	NO encienda, apague ni intente mover u operar equipos cerca del punto donde se rompió la línea o se produjo el escape.
*	NO entre en un área donde haya un escape de gas natural.
*	NO permita que otras personas entren en dicha área.
*	NO deje el lugar del incidente hasta que llegue la ayuda.
*	DESPEJE el área y evite que otras personas entren en ella.
*	ELIMINE las fuentes de combustión, como chispas o llamas, cerca de la atmósfera gaseosa.

Si desea más información sobre los tipos de tuberías de gas usados por SWG o sobre cómo identificar instalaciones de gas, o si tiene preguntas, llame a la oficina de SWG más cercana. En nuestra hoja de datos de seguridad de material (MSDS), puede encontrar más información sobre la seguridad con el gas natural. Esta se encuentra en www.swgas.com/emergencysafety <http://www.swgas.com/emergencysafety> .






Favor de hacer llegar al excavador correspondiente.

Plan Review Correction Task Assignment

Attention Steve:

This email serves as notification that the plan review for project number (251389-LPSG) is complete and corrections are required. The plans and comments can now be accessed by clicking on the "Login to ProjectDox" link below. You should have already received an email notification from "SB1598 DSD/DSD/PHX@PHXENT" containing additional information regarding this plan review. If you need further assistance please call the Payments and Submittals section at 602-534-5934.

Effective December 31, 2012, State law A.R.S. Subsection 9-836 requires that no more than two substantive reviews are completed by a jurisdiction before the plans are either approved and a permit is ready to be issued, or the plans are denied and the review must start over. With these limitations on plan review, the Planning & Development Department can no longer put plans on hold or perform a third review to allow redesign after the first review. If any part of the construction plans are revised or redesigned after the first comprehensive plan review, the permit will be either denied and the applicant must resubmit, or the applicant may obtain a permit for the initial design and then submit revisions as a separate submittal. Please visit our website for more information: phoenix.gov/pdd/licensetimes.html. 

Plan review correction cycles and plan approvals are valid for 180 days. Application for extension must be made and the fee paid PRIOR to the expiration date or a new plan review submittal and fee will be required. 

IMPORTANT NOTE: Completing the assigned ProjectDox WorkFlow Portal task sends the project back to the City of Phoenix. If the applicant does not complete their assigned task, City staff will not receive notice the project requires action.

Proposed sign A exceeds the maximum height allowed by sign code 705 table D1, commercial land use. Please lower overall sign height to 16 feet. To keep as proposed, submit for design review. the fee is $150; the review time is 2 weeks and requires a written narrative.

Thank you,

body:
Ticket Status Notification

Ticket Information

Ticket Number: 2025111900878

GLENDALE, MARICOPA, AZ United States

Phone: 6022424488

Fax/Email:  / STEVE@CHRISTYSIGNS.COM

 




Reason for Notification

Notification Type: Bore Standby        Date: 11/19/2025

You have indicated on the Locate Request(s) that you intend to use Boring in your work area. To ensure the integrity of our system, Southwest Gas is requesting you call us prior to exposing our facilities. Southwest Gas requires a representative to be present to verify our facilities prior to boring across or parallel within 5-feet of Southwest Gas facilities. This is to confirm that you have in fact exposed our line and confirm the line depth to assure a safe bore operation by positive identification of our facilities. Call to schedule a standby a minimum of two hours prior to work identified above.

Notify an SWG representative when boring parallel to any Southwest Gas facilities within 5-feet of the bore. This applies to vertical boring as well.

1.	Notify an SWG representative when boring across any Southwest Gas facilities.

2.	Pothole any gas facilities within 24-inches of the proposed bore path.

3.	Hand digging is required within 24-inches of the gas facility markings, and all gas facilities must be identified, protected, and exposed during any boring operations.

4.	Before the excavation, schedule a Bore Standby with a SWG representative to be present to verify the buried facilities and monitor the boring activities.

Please contact your local SWG field office to schedule a Bore Standby with a Southwest Gas representative a

minimum of 2 hours prior.

 602-484-5085

 For more information regarding safe digging practices, please visit swgas.com

Locate Requester will notify its employees and any of their subcontractors of these requirements.

If you have any questions or need any assistance, please notify Southwest Gas immediately.

Southwest Gas Corporation Business Hours (Mon-Fri between 600 a.m. & 2:30 p.m.) After Hours Emergency: 877-860-6020

EXCAVATOR PRECAUTIONARY GUIDELINES

 

This information is to assist excavators in the proper identification of gas facilities, and precautions to be taken when working around gas facilities.  The information provided here is not to be considered all-inclusive. All excavators digging within the vicinity of gas pipelines must protect the pipelines in accordance with the applicable One-Call law. The following are guidelines that will assist you in protecting the public, you, and the gas facilities.

If any gas pipelines are damaged, federal law requires that you call Southwest Gas Corporation (SWG). Additionally, if the damage results in the escape of gas, you must call the Emergency Number 911.  Note: Damage includes damage to steel pipeline coatings, gouges in plastic pipe, damaged tracer wire, dents or scrapes in steel pipe, etc.

Gas pipeline markers are used to alert the public that gas pipelines are buried in the general area. These markers may or may not be placed directly over the gas facility. When performing an excavation within 10’ of a “High Pressure” marked facility, please contact SWG to arrange for stand by personnel to be present.

 

PLASTIC PIPELINES:  Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) pipe is one type of plastic pipe used in the SWG gas distribution system.  PVC may be faint yellow, gray or white in color and range in size from ½" to 2" in diameter.  PVC is not as flexible as the polyethylene (PE) pipe that SWG installs today. The integrity of PVC can be compromised if scratched or subjected to external loads and/or stresses.  PE is another type of plastic pipe used in SWG’s system.  PE may be found in various colors and range in size from ½" to 8" in diameter.  Although PE is a more flexible material, its integrity can be compromised if scratched or nicked.  Many plastic gas pipelines are installed with a tracer wire in order to locate the facility.  If a tracer wire is or has been severed or damaged, call SWG.  We will repair the damaged wire at no charge.

 

STEEL PIPELINES: Steel gas pipelines, used in both SWG gas distribution and high-pressure transmission systems, range in size from ½" to 24" in diameter and are also susceptible to damage.  Dents and gouges in the steel will affect the integrity of the pipe, so precautionary measures must be taken during excavation.  Steel pipelines are protected with an approved coating material that helps prevent deterioration of the pipe and can be found in various colors.  If during excavation the coating is torn or damaged, contact SWG immediately to facilitate the repairs at no charge.  Call us before disturbing any mastic coating on active or abandoned steel pipe.  The coating is likely to contain regulated asbestos fibers that can be harmful to your employees.

 

Typically, most gas pipes have specific identification markings on them or on the coating.  Care should be taken to support and protect all gas pipelines, as required by law, when exposed or crossed during excavation activities.  Additionally, care must be taken while exposing existing facilities as they may or may not have padding and shading surrounding them as outlined below.  If any gas pipeline is damaged, call SWG immediately to facilitate the proper pipeline repairs.  When excavations have been completed, gas pipelines must be properly padded, shaded, and backfilled per SWG standards, as shown in the drawing below.  SWG specifications for padding and shading material call for it to be able to sift through a 3/8" screen and be smooth and relatively rock free.  Excavations must be compacted to meet the requirements of local authorities.  During backfill activities it is very important to compact the soil beneath the gas pipe to properly support it. Also, it is important to avoid mechanically compacting the soil directly over the gas pipe to eliminate any unnecessary external stresses.  Steps must be taken during this process to protect the gas pipeline from excessive external loadings.  If other utilities or substructures are to be installed in the same excavation as a gas pipeline, the proper clearances shown in the drawing must be maintained.

If at any time during excavation activities you smell gas, call SWG and 911.

*	DO NOT attempt to control or stop the flow of natural gas, or make repairs.
*	DO NOT turn on, turn off, or attempt to move or operate equipment near the line break or point of leakage.
*	DO NOT enter the area where the natural gas is escaping.
*	DO NOT allow others to enter the area.
*	DO NOT leave the scene of the incident until assistance has arrived.
*	DO secure the area and prevent others from entering.
*	DO eliminate sources of ignition, such as sparks or flames, near the gaseous atmosphere.

For more information on the types of gas pipe used by SWG, positive identification of gas facilities, or if you have any questions, please contact the SWG office nearest you. Additional information on natural gas safety is included in our Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) located at www.swgas.com/emergencysafety <http://www.swgas.com/emergencysafety> .

Please forward to the appropriate excavator.




Esta información tiene como objetivo ayudar a los excavadores a identificar adecuadamente las instalaciones de gas y a conocer las precauciones que deben tener cuando trabajan cerca de ellas. La información aquí provista no es exhaustiva. Todos los excavadores que trabajen en cercanías de gasoductos deben protegerlos de acuerdo con la ley vigente sobre excavaciones. Las siguientes son pautas que lo ayudarán a proteger al público, a usted mismo y a las instalaciones de gas.

Si el gasoducto está dañado, la ley federal exige que llame a Southwest Gas Corporation (SWG). Además, si el daño causa un escape de gas, debe llamar al número para emergencias 911. Nota: Los daños pueden ser daños en el recubrimiento de las tuberías de acero, aberturas en las tuberías plásticas, daños en el alambre de rastreo, mellas o raspaduras en las tuberías de acero, etc.

 

Se usan señales para advertir al público de que hay gasoductos enterrados en el área. Estas señales pueden ponerse directamente sobre la instalación de gas o no. Cuando se lleva a cabo una excavación dentro de los 10’ de una instalación señalizada como “High Pressure” (de alta presión), comuníquese con SWG para que envíen personal de respaldo.

TUBERÍAS PLÁSTICAS Las tuberías de policloruro de vinilo (PVC) son un tipo de tubería plástica que SWG usa en el sistema de distribución. Las tuberías de PVC pueden ser de color amarillo claro, gris o blanco, y su tamaño puede ir desde ½” hasta 2” de diámetro. Las tuberías de PVC no son tan flexibles como las de polietileno (PE) que SWG instala hoy. El PVC puede arruinarse si se raya o se somete a pesos o tensiones extremos. Las tuberías de PE son otro tipo de tuberías plásticas que SWG usa en su sistema. Las tuberías de PE pueden ser de varios colores, y su tamaño va desde ½” hasta 8” de diámetro. Aunque el PE es un material más flexible, puede arruinarse si se raya o corta. Muchos gasoductos de plástico se instalan con un alambre de rastreo para ubicar la instalación. Si el alambre de rastreo se corta o daña, llame a SWG. Lo repararemos sin cargo.

 

TUBERÍAS DE ACERO Las tuberías de gas de acero, usadas por SWG tanto para la distribución de gas como para los sistemas de transmisión a alta presión, varían en tamaño desde 1/2" hasta 24" de diámetro y también son susceptibles a los daños. Las mellas y aberturas en el acero pueden afectar la integridad de la tubería. Por eso, deben tomarse medidas de precaución durante la excavación. Las tuberías de acero se protegen con un material de recubrimiento aprobado que ayuda a prevenir su deterioro y puede ser de varios colores. Si durante la excavación el recubrimiento se desprende o daña, comuníquese con SWG de inmediato para facilitar las reparaciones sin cargo. Llámenos antes de quitar cualquier recubrimiento de masilla de una tubería de acero activa o abandonada. Es posible que el recubrimiento contenga fibras de amianto reglamentario que pueden ser dañinas para sus empleados.

 

En general, las tuberías de gas tienen marcas de identificación específicas sobre ellas o sobre el recubrimiento. Debe tenerse precaución y sostener y proteger todos los gasoductos, según lo requiera la ley, cuando se expongan o crucen durante la excavación. Además, debe tenerse cuidado al exponer instalaciones existentes, ya que pueden o no, tener relleno a su alrededor, como se detalla más abajo. Si un gasoducto está dañado, llame a SWG de inmediato para facilitar las reparaciones necesarias. Cuando finalicen las excavaciones, los gasoductos deben ser rellenados según las normas de SWG, como se muestra en el dibujo más abajo. Las especificaciones de SWG para el material de relleno indican que este debe poder pasar a través de un tamiz de 3/8”, ser suave y estar relativamente libre de escombros.  Las excavaciones deben ser compactadas para cumplir con los requisitos de las autoridades locales. Durante el rellenado, es muy importante compactar el suelo bajo el gasoducto, a fin de sujetarlo apropiadamente. También es importante evitar compactar mecánicamente el suelo que está sobre el gasoducto para eliminar tensiones externas innecesarias. Deben tomarse medidas durante este proceso para proteger el gasoducto de cargas externas excesivas. Si se deben instalar otros servicios o subestructuras en la misma excavación del gasoducto, deben respetarse las distancias que se muestran en el dibujo.

Si en cualquier momento durante la excavación percibe olor a gas, llame a SWG y al 911.

*	NO intente controlar ni parar el flujo de gas natural ni de hacer reparaciones.
*	NO encienda, apague ni intente mover u operar equipos cerca del punto donde se rompió la línea o se produjo el escape.
*	NO entre en un área donde haya un escape de gas natural.
*	NO permita que otras personas entren en dicha área.
*	NO deje el lugar del incidente hasta que llegue la ayuda.
*	DESPEJE el área y evite que otras personas entren en ella.
*	ELIMINE las fuentes de combustión, como chispas o llamas, cerca de la atmósfera gaseosa.

Si desea más información sobre los tipos de tuberías de gas usados por SWG o sobre cómo identificar instalaciones de gas, o si tiene preguntas, llame a la oficina de SWG más cercana. En nuestra hoja de datos de seguridad de material (MSDS), puede encontrar más información sobre la seguridad con el gas natural. Esta se encuentra en www.swgas.com/emergencysafety <http://www.swgas.com/emergencysafety> .






Favor de hacer llegar al excavador correspondiente.

subject: Dig Safely Near Southwest Gas Pipelines

THANK YOU for using 811 to submit a locate ticket for work near Southwest Gas pipelines. 

To help you avoid pipeline emergencies, follow these simple steps:

1.    Survey and mark your proposed dig area with white paint.

2.    Wait the required time. This is 2 working days, NOT including the date of notification.

3.    Respect the marks. Ensure all utility owners have responded before digging.  

4.   Contact Southwest Gas and request a monitor prior to bore operations or working within 10 ft. of high-pressure facilities. 

5.   Dig Carefully.  Watch this short video <https://www.swgas.com/en/excavator-safety?utm_source=link&utm_medium=website_email&utm_campaign=Damage_Prevention_Safe_Digging_Video&utm_id=Perseverant&utm_term=>  to learn best practices when digging around underground natural gas lines.

6.    Follow safe excavation laws for the state you're working in. 

Always dig with care! Damage to natural gas lines can result in costly repairs, service outages, and project downtime, as well as severe injury and/or death.  

To report a pipeline emergency or odor of natural gas, call 911 and Southwest Gas at 877-860-6020.

Thanks for working safely near our facilities.

subject: Ticket Notifications 202511130581: Item created, triggered per rule: CAD -  Southwest
body:
Ticket Status Notification

Ticket Information

Ticket Number: 2025111301161

Ticket Location: 1575 E BASELINE RD
PHOENIX, MARICOPA, AZ United States
33.3773466568983, -112.047993913967 

Due Date: 11/17/2025 7:00 PM ET

Company: CHRISTY SIGNS

Phone: 6022424488

Fax/Email:  / STEVE@CHRISTYSIGNS.COM

 




Reason for Notification

Notification Type: Bore Standby        Date: 11/13/2025

You have indicated on the Locate Request(s) that you intend to use Boring in your work area. To ensure the integrity of our system, Southwest Gas is requesting you call us prior to exposing our facilities. Southwest Gas requires a representative to be present to verify our facilities prior to boring across or parallel within 5-feet of Southwest Gas facilities. This is to confirm that you have in fact exposed our line and confirm the line depth to assure a safe bore operation by positive identification of our facilities. Call to schedule a standby a minimum of two hours prior to work identified above.

Notify an SWG representative when boring parallel to any Southwest Gas facilities within 5-feet of the bore. This applies to vertical boring as well.

1.	Notify an SWG representative when boring across any Southwest Gas facilities.

2.	Pothole any gas facilities within 24-inches of the proposed bore path.

3.	Hand digging is required within 24-inches of the gas facility markings, and all gas facilities must be identified, protected, and exposed during any boring operations.

4.	Before the excavation, schedule a Bore Standby with a SWG representative to be present to verify the buried facilities and monitor the boring activities.

Please contact your local SWG field office to schedule a Bore Standby with a Southwest Gas representative a

minimum of 2 hours prior.

 602-484-5086

 For more information regarding safe digging practices, please visit swgas.com

Locate Requester will notify its employees and any of their subcontractors of these requirements.

If you have any questions or need any assistance, please notify Southwest Gas immediately.

Southwest Gas Corporation Business Hours (Mon-Fri between 600 a.m. & 2:30 p.m.) After Hours Emergency: 877-860-6020

EXCAVATOR PRECAUTIONARY GUIDELINES

 

This information is to assist excavators in the proper identification of gas facilities, and precautions to be taken when working around gas facilities.  The information provided here is not to be considered all-inclusive. All excavators digging within the vicinity of gas pipelines must protect the pipelines in accordance with the applicable One-Call law. The following are guidelines that will assist you in protecting the public, you, and the gas facilities.

If any gas pipelines are damaged, federal law requires that you call Southwest Gas Corporation (SWG). Additionally, if the damage results in the escape of gas, you must call the Emergency Number 911.  Note: Damage includes damage to steel pipeline coatings, gouges in plastic pipe, damaged tracer wire, dents or scrapes in steel pipe, etc.

Gas pipeline markers are used to alert the public that gas pipelines are buried in the general area. These markers may or may not be placed directly over the gas facility. When performing an excavation within 10’ of a “High Pressure” marked facility, please contact SWG to arrange for stand by personnel to be present.

 

PLASTIC PIPELINES:  Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC) pipe is one type of plastic pipe used in the SWG gas distribution system.  PVC may be faint yellow, gray or white in color and range in size from ½" to 2" in diameter.  PVC is not as flexible as the polyethylene (PE) pipe that SWG installs today. The integrity of PVC can be compromised if scratched or subjected to external loads and/or stresses.  PE is another type of plastic pipe used in SWG’s system.  PE may be found in various colors and range in size from ½" to 8" in diameter.  Although PE is a more flexible material, its integrity can be compromised if scratched or nicked.  Many plastic gas pipelines are installed with a tracer wire in order to locate the facility.  If a tracer wire is or has been severed or damaged, call SWG.  We will repair the damaged wire at no charge.

 

STEEL PIPELINES: Steel gas pipelines, used in both SWG gas distribution and high-pressure transmission systems, range in size from ½" to 24" in diameter and are also susceptible to damage.  Dents and gouges in the steel will affect the integrity of the pipe, so precautionary measures must be taken during excavation.  Steel pipelines are protected with an approved coating material that helps prevent deterioration of the pipe and can be found in various colors.  If during excavation the coating is torn or damaged, contact SWG immediately to facilitate the repairs at no charge.  Call us before disturbing any mastic coating on active or abandoned steel pipe.  The coating is likely to contain regulated asbestos fibers that can be harmful to your employees.

 

Typically, most gas pipes have specific identification markings on them or on the coating.  Care should be taken to support and protect all gas pipelines, as required by law, when exposed or crossed during excavation activities.  Additionally, care must be taken while exposing existing facilities as they may or may not have padding and shading surrounding them as outlined below.  If any gas pipeline is damaged, call SWG immediately to facilitate the proper pipeline repairs.  When excavations have been completed, gas pipelines must be properly padded, shaded, and backfilled per SWG standards, as shown in the drawing below.  SWG specifications for padding and shading material call for it to be able to sift through a 3/8" screen and be smooth and relatively rock free.  Excavations must be compacted to meet the requirements of local authorities.  During backfill activities it is very important to compact the soil beneath the gas pipe to properly support it. Also, it is important to avoid mechanically compacting the soil directly over the gas pipe to eliminate any unnecessary external stresses.  Steps must be taken during this process to protect the gas pipeline from excessive external loadings.  If other utilities or substructures are to be installed in the same excavation as a gas pipeline, the proper clearances shown in the drawing must be maintained.

If at any time during excavation activities you smell gas, call SWG and 911.

*	DO NOT attempt to control or stop the flow of natural gas, or make repairs.
*	DO NOT turn on, turn off, or attempt to move or operate equipment near the line break or point of leakage.
*	DO NOT enter the area where the natural gas is escaping.
*	DO NOT allow others to enter the area.
*	DO NOT leave the scene of the incident until assistance has arrived.
*	DO secure the area and prevent others from entering.
*	DO eliminate sources of ignition, such as sparks or flames, near the gaseous atmosphere.

For more information on the types of gas pipe used by SWG, positive identification of gas facilities, or if you have any questions, please contact the SWG office nearest you. Additional information on natural gas safety is included in our Material Safety Data Sheet (MSDS) located at www.swgas.com/emergencysafety <http://www.swgas.com/emergencysafety> .

Please forward to the appropriate excavator.




Esta información tiene como objetivo ayudar a los excavadores a identificar adecuadamente las instalaciones de gas y a conocer las precauciones que deben tener cuando trabajan cerca de ellas. La información aquí provista no es exhaustiva. Todos los excavadores que trabajen en cercanías de gasoductos deben protegerlos de acuerdo con la ley vigente sobre excavaciones. Las siguientes son pautas que lo ayudarán a proteger al público, a usted mismo y a las instalaciones de gas.

Si el gasoducto está dañado, la ley federal exige que llame a Southwest Gas Corporation (SWG). Además, si el daño causa un escape de gas, debe llamar al número para emergencias 911. Nota: Los daños pueden ser daños en el recubrimiento de las tuberías de acero, aberturas en las tuberías plásticas, daños en el alambre de rastreo, mellas o raspaduras en las tuberías de acero, etc.

 

Se usan señales para advertir al público de que hay gasoductos enterrados en el área. Estas señales pueden ponerse directamente sobre la instalación de gas o no. Cuando se lleva a cabo una excavación dentro de los 10’ de una instalación señalizada como “High Pressure” (de alta presión), comuníquese con SWG para que envíen personal de respaldo.

TUBERÍAS PLÁSTICAS Las tuberías de policloruro de vinilo (PVC) son un tipo de tubería plástica que SWG usa en el sistema de distribución. Las tuberías de PVC pueden ser de color amarillo claro, gris o blanco, y su tamaño puede ir desde ½” hasta 2” de diámetro. Las tuberías de PVC no son tan flexibles como las de polietileno (PE) que SWG instala hoy. El PVC puede arruinarse si se raya o se somete a pesos o tensiones extremos. Las tuberías de PE son otro tipo de tuberías plásticas que SWG usa en su sistema. Las tuberías de PE pueden ser de varios colores, y su tamaño va desde ½” hasta 8” de diámetro. Aunque el PE es un material más flexible, puede arruinarse si se raya o corta. Muchos gasoductos de plástico se instalan con un alambre de rastreo para ubicar la instalación. Si el alambre de rastreo se corta o daña, llame a SWG. Lo repararemos sin cargo.

 

TUBERÍAS DE ACERO Las tuberías de gas de acero, usadas por SWG tanto para la distribución de gas como para los sistemas de transmisión a alta presión, varían en tamaño desde 1/2" hasta 24" de diámetro y también son susceptibles a los daños. Las mellas y aberturas en el acero pueden afectar la integridad de la tubería. Por eso, deben tomarse medidas de precaución durante la excavación. Las tuberías de acero se protegen con un material de recubrimiento aprobado que ayuda a prevenir su deterioro y puede ser de varios colores. Si durante la excavación el recubrimiento se desprende o daña, comuníquese con SWG de inmediato para facilitar las reparaciones sin cargo. Llámenos antes de quitar cualquier recubrimiento de masilla de una tubería de acero activa o abandonada. Es posible que el recubrimiento contenga fibras de amianto reglamentario que pueden ser dañinas para sus empleados.

 

En general, las tuberías de gas tienen marcas de identificación específicas sobre ellas o sobre el recubrimiento. Debe tenerse precaución y sostener y proteger todos los gasoductos, según lo requiera la ley, cuando se expongan o crucen durante la excavación. Además, debe tenerse cuidado al exponer instalaciones existentes, ya que pueden o no, tener relleno a su alrededor, como se detalla más abajo. Si un gasoducto está dañado, llame a SWG de inmediato para facilitar las reparaciones necesarias. Cuando finalicen las excavaciones, los gasoductos deben ser rellenados según las normas de SWG, como se muestra en el dibujo más abajo. Las especificaciones de SWG para el material de relleno indican que este debe poder pasar a través de un tamiz de 3/8”, ser suave y estar relativamente libre de escombros.  Las excavaciones deben ser compactadas para cumplir con los requisitos de las autoridades locales. Durante el rellenado, es muy importante compactar el suelo bajo el gasoducto, a fin de sujetarlo apropiadamente. También es importante evitar compactar mecánicamente el suelo que está sobre el gasoducto para eliminar tensiones externas innecesarias. Deben tomarse medidas durante este proceso para proteger el gasoducto de cargas externas excesivas. Si se deben instalar otros servicios o subestructuras en la misma excavación del gasoducto, deben respetarse las distancias que se muestran en el dibujo.

Si en cualquier momento durante la excavación percibe olor a gas, llame a SWG y al 911.

*	NO intente controlar ni parar el flujo de gas natural ni de hacer reparaciones.
*	NO encienda, apague ni intente mover u operar equipos cerca del punto donde se rompió la línea o se produjo el escape.
*	NO entre en un área donde haya un escape de gas natural.
*	NO permita que otras personas entren en dicha área.
*	NO deje el lugar del incidente hasta que llegue la ayuda.
*	DESPEJE el área y evite que otras personas entren en ella.
*	ELIMINE las fuentes de combustión, como chispas o llamas, cerca de la atmósfera gaseosa.

Si desea más información sobre los tipos de tuberías de gas usados por SWG o sobre cómo identificar instalaciones de gas, o si tiene preguntas, llame a la oficina de SWG más cercana. En nuestra hoja de datos de seguridad de material (MSDS), puede encontrar más información sobre la seguridad con el gas natural. Esta se encuentra en www.swgas.com/emergencysafety <http://www.swgas.com/emergencysafety> .






Favor de hacer llegar al excavador correspondiente.

From: Steve Skye <steve@christysigns.com <mailto:steve@christysigns.com> >
Sent: Thursday, November 6, 2025 9:14:33 AM
To: Rocky Marsh <rocky@christysigns.com <mailto:rocky@christysigns.com> >
Subject: Signage Limitations for Wendler Parcels – City of Tempe (GID Zoning) 

 

Hi Rocky,

I wanted to update you on the signage restrictions for the Wendler parcels (4415 & 4625 S Wendler Dr, Tempe), based on our review of the City of Tempe Zoning and Development Code and confirmation from Mike Scarpitta of the Tempe Sign Department.


Both parcels are zoned GID (General Industrial District) and are not part of any PAD or Development Plan. As such, they are limited to standard monument-style freestanding signs under Tempe ZDC §§ 4-901–4-904.

Here are the key points:

*	Maximum sign height: 8 ft
*	Maximum sign area: 24 sq ft per face
*	Type: Monument or architectural base design (masonry/stucco finish to match building)
*	Freeway/high-profile signs: Only permitted through a recorded Development Plan or PAD overlay—these Wendler parcels do not qualify under current zoning.
*	Address numerals: Minimum 6″ high required on the base.


Mike confirmed that the larger “freeway monument” signs along the I-10 corridor were approved decades ago as part of their original Development Plans and are effectively grandfathered. 

The Wendler properties were not included in those agreements, so the City will enforce the 8' / 24 sq ft limitation.


Attached is the full Sign Ordinance Report – Tempe Wendler Parcels (GID) summarizing these findings, citations, and code references for our records.


Best regards,

 

Steve Skye

Your submittal to the Town of Gilbert have been reviewed and your Plan Case number is PDR-2025-00158. Please visit https://onestopshop.gilbertaz.gov/ to upload exhibits and pay the fee by doing the following: 

1. Navigate to the Plan Case number

2. To upload exhibits, click on Attachments tab. Use the drop-down menu to select the type of exhibit and then click the + sign to browse for the exhibit. Refer to the checklist for the appropriate application here: https://www.gilbertaz.gov/departments/development-services/planning/forms-fees-applications . ***Planners will not be notified of uploads if any boxes are left empty, delaying the review process.

3. Fees are due now. Click on the Pay Now button to pay the fees. Processing will not begin until fees are paid in full. Please note if fees are not paid within 30 days, the case will be cancelled without further notice.

Best regards,

Gilbert Planning Services Division.

I can’t believe Q4 is already here, and that means it’s time to remind end-users about the IRS 179 Tax Credit, which applies not only to digital displays but to the entire sign package.




For example, if a sign package costs $50,000—including installation, fabrication, permitting, LED display, and your markup—the end-user can receive a tax savings of $17,500. This reduces the total cost to just $32,500—a huge savings!

Hi Sarah,

Thanks again for marking up the brand book—that’s exactly what we needed to keep things moving. I’ve attached a one-page Information Sheet on NEC 600 for reference, which summarizes the code requirements inspectors are looking for.  To clarify your two questions:

3. Dedicated 20A Branch Circuit
You’re right—the electrician ultimately provides and labels the circuit. But under NEC 600.5(A), every sign must be supplied by a dedicated 20A branch circuit

Inspectors want to see this noted on the plans, so it doesn’t get overlooked in the field, even if it isn’t a fabrication detail.


4. Grounding/Bonding
This is about ensuring all metal parts of the sign and raceways are tied together and properly grounded. NEC 600.7 requires metallic sign enclosures and equipment to be bonded to ground.  In practice, this means including a note that a grounding conductor and bonding jumpers will be installed so the sign is safe under fault conditions.


So, while these items are implemented by the electrician, the city expects them to be called out on the drawings for code compliance.


Please see the attached information sheet for a clear summary of the requirements.


Best regards,

Hi Sarah,

Thanks again for marking up the brand book—that’s exactly what we needed to keep things moving. I’ve attached a one-page Information Sheet on NEC 600 for reference, which summarizes the code requirements inspectors are looking for.  To clarify your two questions:

3. Dedicated 20A Branch Circuit
You’re right—the electrician ultimately provides and labels the circuit. But under NEC 600.5(A), every sign must be supplied by a dedicated 20A branch circuit

Inspectors want to see this noted on the plans, so it doesn’t get overlooked in the field, even if it isn’t a fabrication detail.


4. Grounding/Bonding
This is about ensuring all metal parts of the sign and raceways are tied together and properly grounded. NEC 600.7 requires metallic sign enclosures and equipment to be bonded to ground.  In practice, this means including a note that a grounding conductor and bonding jumpers will be installed so the sign is safe under fault conditions.


So, while these items are implemented by the electrician, the city expects them to be called out on the drawings for code compliance.


Please see the attached information sheet for a clear summary of the requirements.


Best regards,

Effective December 31, 2012, State law A.R.S. Subsection 9-835 requires that no more than two substantive reviews are completed by a jurisdiction before the plans are either approved and a permit is ready to be issued, or the plans are denied and the review must start over.  With these limitations on plan review, the Planning & Development Department can no longer put plans on hold or perform a third review to allow redesign after the first review.  If any part of the construction plans are revised or redesigned after the first comprehensive plan review, the permit will be either denied and the applicant must resubmit, or the applicant may obtain a permit for the initial design and then submit revisions as a separate submittal.  

All Single Family Residential projects/subdivisions are exempt from this law if submitted for first review after September 14, 2013. 

Please visit our website for more information: https://www.phoenix.gov/pddsite/Pages/pddlicensetimes.aspx.

subject: Re: Power Requirements and Electrical Coordination – Freestanding Sign (10/23/25)
body:
Thank you for the information. 

On Thu, Oct 23, 2025 at 1:17 PM Steve Skye <steve@christysigns.com <mailto:steve@christysigns.com> > wrote:


	Hi Aaron,
	
	

	I’m glad to hear the artwork and proposed design meet your expectations.

	
	For the new freestanding sign, a dedicated 120V / 20-amp circuit will be required at the base of the sign. This circuit will supply power for the internal LED illumination and must comply with the National Electrical Code (NEC) Article 600 (Electric Signs and Outline Lighting).

	Key provisions include:

	*	NEC 600.5(A) – Each sign must be supplied by its own branch circuit.
	*	NEC 600.6(A)(1) – A disconnecting means must be installed within sight of the sign.
	*	NEC 600.7(A) – Proper grounding and bonding are required for all metallic parts.

	
	Our installation will include a junction box and weather-rated disconnect switch mounted at the base of the sign.
	
	We recommend having your electrician provide:

	*	A dedicated 20A circuit from the building’s main panel to the sign base.
	*	A time clock or photo control near the breaker panel where the power run originates — this allows automatic on/off control for the sign lighting.

	
	Once the circuit is in place, our team will make the final internal connections during installation and test all components.

	
	Please let me know if you’d like us to coordinate directly with your electrician or provide a connection diagram for reference.

	
	Warm regards,

	 

	Steve Skye

Plan Review Correction Task Assignment

Attention Steve:

This email serves as notification that the plan review for project number (251110-LPSG ADA2) is complete and corrections are required. The plans and comments can now be accessed by clicking on the "Login to ProjectDox" link below. You should have already received an email notification from "SB1598 DSD/DSD/PHX@PHXENT" containing additional information regarding this plan review. If you need further assistance please call the Payments and Submittals section at 602-534-5934.

Effective December 31, 2012, State law A.R.S. Subsection 9-836 requires that no more than two substantive reviews are completed by a jurisdiction before the plans are either approved and a permit is ready to be issued, or the plans are denied and the review must start over. With these limitations on plan review, the Planning & Development Department can no longer put plans on hold or perform a third review to allow redesign after the first review. If any part of the construction plans are revised or redesigned after the first comprehensive plan review, the permit will be either denied and the applicant must resubmit, or the applicant may obtain a permit for the initial design and then submit revisions as a separate submittal. Please visit our website for more information: phoenix.gov/pdd/licensetimes.html. 

Plan review correction cycles and plan approvals are valid for 180 days. Application for extension must be made and the fee paid PRIOR to the expiration date or a new plan review submittal and fee will be required. 

IMPORTANT NOTE: Completing the assigned ProjectDox WorkFlow Portal task sends the project back to the City of Phoenix. If the applicant does not complete their assigned task, City staff will not receive notice the project requires action.

Effective December 31, 2012, State law A.R.S. Subsection 9-835 requires that no more than two substantive reviews are completed by a jurisdiction before the plans are either approved and a permit is ready to be issued, or the plans are denied and the review must start over.  With these limitations on plan review, the Planning & Development Department can no longer put plans on hold or perform a third review to allow redesign after the first review.  If any part of the construction plans are revised or redesigned after the first comprehensive plan review, the permit will be either denied and the applicant must resubmit, or the applicant may obtain a permit for the initial design and then submit revisions as a separate submittal.  

All Single Family Residential projects/subdivisions are exempt from this law if submitted for first review after September 14, 2013. 

Please visit our website for more information: https://www.phoenix.gov/pddsite/Pages/pddlicensetimes.aspx.

Effective December 31, 2012, State law A.R.S. Subsection 9-835 requires that no more than two substantive reviews are completed by a jurisdiction before the plans are either approved and a permit is ready to be issued, or the plans are denied and the review must start over.  With these limitations on plan review, the Planning & Development Department can no longer put plans on hold or perform a third review to allow redesign after the first review.  If any part of the construction plans are revised or redesigned after the first comprehensive plan review, the permit will be either denied and the applicant must resubmit, or the applicant may obtain a permit for the initial design and then submit revisions as a separate submittal.  

All Single Family Residential projects/subdivisions are exempt from this law if submitted for first review after September 14, 2013. 

Please visit our website for more information: https://www.phoenix.gov/pddsite/Pages/pddlicensetimes.aspx. 

Plan review correction cycles and plan approvals are valid for 180 days. Application for extension must be made and the fee paid PRIOR to the expiration date or a new plan review submittal and fee will be required.

subject: Metal Spotlight! - The more you know!
body:
Are Metal Storage Unit Kits Cheaper Than Building Your Self?
When it comes to adding storage space to your property, the decision between purchasing a metal storage unit kit or building one from scratch involves numerous considerations. Cost often tops the list of concerns for most property owners. While the DIY approach might seem like the obvious money-saving choice at first glance, the reality is more nuanced. This comprehensive analysis explores whether metal storage unit kits <https://durobuildings.com/>  truly offer better value than building a storage solution yourself.
The Initial Cost Comparison
The upfront price tag represents just one dimension of the total cost. Metal storage unit kits <https://durobuildings.com/steel-warehouses/>  typically range from $5,000.00 to $50,000.00 depending on size, quality, and features. This price usually includes all necessary materials pre-cut to specifications, fasteners, and detailed assembly instructions.
Building a comparable structure from scratch requires purchasing raw materials such as lumber, metal sheeting, concrete for the foundation, insulation, and various hardware components. While buying materials individually might seem less expensive initially, several hidden factors come into play that can quickly escalate costs.
Raw materials purchased at retail prices without contractor discounts often end up costing more than the bulk-purchased, precision-manufactured components in kits. Additionally, DIY builders frequently underestimate material needs, resulting in multiple trips to hardware stores and accumulating expenses that weren't factored into the original budget.

Time Investment and Opportunity Cost
The DIY approach demands a significant time commitment that many overlook when calculating costs. From researching building techniques and sourcing materials to the actual construction process, a self-built storage unit can consume weeks or even months of your time.
Metal storage kits dramatically reduce this time investment. With pre-cut, pre-drilled components designed for straightforward assembly, most kits can be completed in a weekend or two. This efficiency translates to a substantial opportunity cost saving—time you could spend on income-generating activities or other valuable pursuits.
For business owners or professionals whose time carries a high hourly value, the kit option often represents the more economical choice when factoring in the opportunity cost of extended DIY construction periods.

Expertise and Quality Considerations
Professional engineering underlies every well-designed metal storage kit. These products incorporate proper load calculations, weather resistance features, and structural integrity that DIY designs might lack without professional input.
Self-built structures often suffer from amateur design flaws that compromise durability and functionality. Even experienced DIYers may struggle with the complexities of proper anchoring, sealing, insulation, and ventilation—all crucial elements for a long-lasting storage solution.
The quality differential typically becomes apparent after a few seasons of weather exposure. Kit structures engineered to withstand specific wind loads, snow accumulation, and temperature fluctuations often outlast amateur-built alternatives, providing better long-term value despite potentially higher initial costs.
Permitting and Compliance Factors
Navigating building codes and permit requirements presents another hidden cost center in DIY projects. Self-designed structures frequently encounter compliance issues during inspection, necessitating costly modifications and rework.
Most reputable metal storage unit kits are designed to meet standard building codes across multiple jurisdictions. Manufacturers typically provide engineering specifications and documentation that streamline the permitting process, potentially saving hundreds or even thousands in modification costs and permit resubmission fees.
The simplicity of presenting pre-engineered plans to building departments cannot be overstated—this advantage alone can justify the premium for quality kits in regions with stringent building code enforcement. State engineered stamped drawings can be included in almost all of our designs making it easy to pull those pesky permits! 

Long-Term Value and Maintenance Considerations
The economic equation extends well beyond initial construction. Metal storage kits from reputable manufacturers often include corrosion-resistant finishes, precise sealing elements, and modular components designed for easy replacement if damaged.
DIY structures typically require more frequent maintenance, with earlier onset of issues like rust, leaks, and structural weakness. These ongoing maintenance costs gradually erode any initial savings, particularly when factoring in the value of your time spent on repairs rather than other activities.
Furthermore, professionally designed kits typically offer better resale value and property value enhancement compared to visibly amateur constructions. The clean, professional appearance and known durability of recognized brands translate to tangible property value increases that self-built alternatives rarely match. Don't forget, our steel buildings are backed by a 50 Year Factory backed warranty! 
Environmental and Efficiency Considerations
Modern metal storage kits increasingly incorporate energy-efficient design elements, proper insulation strategies, and materials with reduced environmental impact. The Bottom Line: Total Cost of Ownership

For most property owners, especially those without construction experience or specialized equipment, metal storage unit kits provide superior overall value despite higher upfront costs. The convenience, speed, reliability, and professional results deliver returns that continue accumulating long after the initial construction phase.
The decision ultimately depends on your specific circumstances, including your skill level, available time, tool inventory, and quality expectations. 	And again, I completely understand that review times can vary and that your team is surely managing a large volume of projects. However, at this point, we’re struggling to get clarity on the status, next steps, and expected timing.

	Our signage partner and our team have both been checking the system, but the only update available continues to show “in review.” We’d be grateful for any additional context or insight you could provide—such as where the project currently stands in the process, whether any feedback or revisions are pending, and what typical turnaround times are at this stage.

	My goal isn’t simply to push for speed (although we are eager for signs, at minimum for the bare building) but to better understand the process and expectations so that we can plan future projects more effectively. We want to ensure we’re doing our part to avoid similar bottlenecks and that future openings don’t occur with finished buildings sitting without signage for weeks.

	If there’s a contact within the sign review division who could provide a brief status update or explain typical timelines, I’d deeply appreciate it.

	Alex

body:
Good Morning Scott, 

It’s a big bummer we have been waiting on the City and they have been waiting on us for 5 weeks and none of us knew. 

Also a bummer I had asked if we could just install wall signs because my guess is the hang up was the monument sign. And was told we can separate it without paying new fees and started weeks of time again waiting. But turns out from Tony that’s not true. 

If we install wall signs end of next week that will have been at least 6 weeks - sounds like longer than when we could have installed just them. It’s killing us having that empty building with no signage. 

I’d rather not be involved in the middle of Neon and Christy and then City. 

Please consider the possibility of getting the wall signs up early next week. Is that all you are planning? Or monument too? If monument too we can wait on that and prioritize signs on the building. If all you do is the scooters on both sides and not the smiley on Monday that would be huge. All we want right now is that people know what we are building. It’s big in terms of pre opening marketing that has a real impact on sales. 

Can you please get a team in on Monday? Given the circumstances and unnecessary delays, we would be much appreciative of that extra effort / adjustment in schedule. 

Also do you have a time to give me a call so we can discuss this project more too? We have a third store opening on 19th Ave and Baseline. And then a fourth in Ahwatukee. And I want to dial in our sign process.

Hi Steve,

I spoke with Kimberly Pippin at the Town of Queen Creek this morning (480-358-3003) regarding the awnings. She confirmed that awnings fall under the building permit category, not sign permits, and therefore would require a general contractor’s license.


Since our ROC # 071084 classification does not cover building permits, we would not be able to apply for the awning portion directly.


We will proceed with the flagpole permit (B25-2353), which remains active under the sign permit scope, but the awnings will need to be handled under the building permit process—either by the GC or another licensed contractor qualified for that scope.

	﻿Hi Anthony hope you’re well. Nice to meet you via email.

	We are opening a small Scooter’s Coffee drive thru store this month and still don’t have any signage. It’s our family business. 

	 

	We submitted the permits a few months ago for the signs. Our sign company handled it and I have been asking for updates but they say it hasn’t moved past review since then. Which I thought was odd. So I thought to check in directly.

	Thanks in advance for any assistance!

	We are opening a small Scooter’s Coffee drive thru store this month and still don’t have any signage. It’s our family business.

	﻿Hi Anthony hope you’re well. Nice to meet you via email. 

	 

	Our location is 1575 E Baseline Rd in Phoenixon the corner of 16th St and Baseline. It’s Scooters Store #2597.

	 

	We are opening a small Scooter’s Coffee drive thru store this month and still don’t have any signage. It’s our family business. 

	 

	We submitted the permits a few months ago for the signs. Our sign company handled it and I have been asking for updates but they say it hasn’t moved past review since then. Which I thought was odd. So I thought to check in directly. 

	 

	If someone else is more appropriate to give us an estimated timing we would appreciate it. We would hate to open without signs. :(

	 

	And if you have feedback on how we could have done this better or differently I am all ears. Because we are planning on another store later.

	 

	Thanks in advance for any assistance!

	 

	Kind regards,

	Alex

Alex

Hi Tony and Steve, 

 

Good morning! TGIM!

 

Really appreciate all the quick replies.

 

I am still unclear. It appears its same response that triggered my original inquiry. All I know is that the project is 'in review'. This is what Steve had let me know and he shared that he had no additional info. So, I was reaching out to get more context. I don't have any color or detail, timeline or idea of process. Kind of feels like a black hole, so just seeking to understand. That was my purpose for reaching out. Anthony: is there someone on your team that could help me walk me through where we are at and what to expect next beyond that we are just 'in review' until we are not' which is what I feel is all I have. It's sad seeing our building up with no signage.

 

And again, I completely understand that review times can vary and that your team is surely managing a large volume of projects. However, at this point, we’re struggling to get clarity on the status, next steps, and expected timing.

Our signage partner and our team have both been checking the system, but the only update available continues to show “in review.” We’d be grateful for any additional context or insight you could provide—such as where the project currently stands in the process, whether any feedback or revisions are pending, and what typical turnaround times are at this stage.

My goal isn’t simply to push for speed (although we are eager for signs, at minimum for the bare building) but to better understand the process and expectations so that we can plan future projects more effectively. We want to ensure we’re doing our part to avoid similar bottlenecks and that future openings don’t occur with finished buildings sitting without signage for weeks.

If there’s a contact within the sign review division who could provide a brief status update or explain typical timelines, I’d deeply appreciate it.

Thank you for the important work your team does in keeping the City of Phoenix running smoothly. I know how many requests come through your office, and I’m grateful for your time and any guidance you can offer.

Kind regards,

Alex

Subject: Re: Hi Anthony! Checking in, and introducing myself. LPSG 251110

 

Hi Tony and Steve, 

 

Good morning! TGIM!

 

Really appreciate all the quick replies.

 

I am still unclear. It appears its same response that triggered my original inquiry. All I know is that the project is 'in review'. This is what Steve had let me know and he shared that he had no additional info. So, I was reaching out to get more context. I don't have any color or detail, timeline or idea of process. Kind of feels like a black hole, so just seeking to understand. That was my purpose for reaching out. Anthony: is there someone on your team that could help me walk me through where we are at and what to expect next beyond that we are just 'in review' until we are not' which is what I feel is all I have. It's sad seeing our building up with no signage.

 

And again, I completely understand that review times can vary and that your team is surely managing a large volume of projects. However, at this point, we’re struggling to get clarity on the status, next steps, and expected timing.

Our signage partner and our team have both been checking the system, but the only update available continues to show “in review.” We’d be grateful for any additional context or insight you could provide—such as where the project currently stands in the process, whether any feedback or revisions are pending, and what typical turnaround times are at this stage.

My goal isn’t simply to push for speed (although we are eager for signs, at minimum for the bare building) but to better understand the process and expectations so that we can plan future projects more effectively. We want to ensure we’re doing our part to avoid similar bottlenecks and that future openings don’t occur with finished buildings sitting without signage for weeks.

If there’s a contact within the sign review division who could provide a brief status update or explain typical timelines, I’d deeply appreciate it.

Thank you for the important work your team does in keeping the City of Phoenix running smoothly. I know how many requests come through your office, and I’m grateful for your time and any guidance you can offer.

Kind regards,

Alex

Subject: Re: Hi Anthony! Checking in, and introducing myself. LPSG 251110

 

Hi Tony and Steve, 

 

Good morning! TGIM!

 

Really appreciate all the quick replies.

 

I am still unclear. It appears its same response that triggered my original inquiry. All I know is that the project is 'in review'. This is what Steve had let me know and he shared that he had no additional info. So, I was reaching out to get more context. I don't have any color or detail, timeline or idea of process. Kind of feels like a black hole, so just seeking to understand. That was my purpose for reaching out. Anthony: is there someone on your team that could help me walk me through where we are at and what to expect next beyond that we are just 'in review' until we are not' which is what I feel is all I have. It's sad seeing our building up with no signage.

 

And again, I completely understand that review times can vary and that your team is surely managing a large volume of projects. However, at this point, we’re struggling to get clarity on the status, next steps, and expected timing.

Our signage partner and our team have both been checking the system, but the only update available continues to show “in review.” We’d be grateful for any additional context or insight you could provide—such as where the project currently stands in the process, whether any feedback or revisions are pending, and what typical turnaround times are at this stage.

My goal isn’t simply to push for speed (although we are eager for signs, at minimum for the bare building) but to better understand the process and expectations so that we can plan future projects more effectively. We want to ensure we’re doing our part to avoid similar bottlenecks and that future openings don’t occur with finished buildings sitting without signage for weeks.

If there’s a contact within the sign review division who could provide a brief status update or explain typical timelines, I’d deeply appreciate it.

Thank you for the important work your team does in keeping the City of Phoenix running smoothly. I know how many requests come through your office, and I’m grateful for your time and any guidance you can offer.

Kind regards,

Alex

body:
<https://epr.phoenix.gov/ProjectDox/images/PHXBannerNew.png> 




Plan Review Correction Task Assignment 
________________________________


Attention Steve:

This email serves as notification that the plan review for project number (251110-LPSG) is complete and corrections are required. The plans and comments can now be accessed by clicking on the "Login to ProjectDox" link below. You should have already received an email notification from "SB1598 DSD/DSD/PHX@PHXENT" containing additional information regarding this plan review. If you need further assistance please call the Payments and Submittals section at 602-534-5934.

Effective December 31, 2012, State law A.R.S. Subsection 9-836 requires that no more than two substantive reviews are completed by a jurisdiction before the plans are either approved and a permit is ready to be issued, or the plans are denied and the review must start over. With these limitations on plan review, the Planning & Development Department can no longer put plans on hold or perform a third review to allow redesign after the first review. If any part of the construction plans are revised or redesigned after the first comprehensive plan review, the permit will be either denied and the applicant must resubmit, or the applicant may obtain a permit for the initial design and then submit revisions as a separate submittal. Please visit our website for more information: phoenix.gov/pdd/licensetimes.html. 

Plan review correction cycles and plan approvals are valid for 180 days. Application for extension must be made and the fee paid PRIOR to the expiration date or a new plan review submittal and fee will be required. 

IMPORTANT NOTE: Completing the assigned ProjectDox WorkFlow Portal task sends the project back to the City of Phoenix. If the applicant does not complete their assigned task, City staff will not receive notice the project requires action. 

Project Name:	 251110-LPSG	 
Description:	 Scooters # 2597	 
Task:	 ApplicantResubmit	 
Login to ProjectDox <https://epr.phoenix.gov/ProjectDox>  	

If you have any questions, please contact the Planning and Development Department at 602-534-5934. 

Please do not reply to this email.

Subject: Re: Hi Anthony! Checking in, and introducing myself. LPSG 251110
 
Hi Tony and Steve, 

Good morning! TGIM!

Really appreciate all the quick replies.

I am still unclear. It appears its same response that triggered my original inquiry. All I know is that the project is 'in review'. This is what Steve had let me know and he shared that he had no additional info. So, I was reaching out to get more context. I don't have any color or detail, timeline or idea of process. Kind of feels like a black hole, so just seeking to understand. That was my purpose for reaching out. Anthony: is there someone on your team that could help me walk me through where we are at and what to expect next beyond that we are just 'in review' until we are not' which is what I feel is all I have. It's sad seeing our building up with no signage.

And again, I completely understand that review times can vary and that your team is surely managing a large volume of projects. However, at this point, we’re struggling to get clarity on the status, next steps, and expected timing.
Our signage partner and our team have both been checking the system, but the only update available continues to show “in review.” We’d be grateful for any additional context or insight you could provide—such as where the project currently stands in the process, whether any feedback or revisions are pending, and what typical turnaround times are at this stage.
My goal isn’t simply to push for speed (although we are eager for signs, at minimum for the bare building) but to better understand the process and expectations so that we can plan future projects more effectively. We want to ensure we’re doing our part to avoid similar bottlenecks and that future openings don’t occur with finished buildings sitting without signage for weeks.
If there’s a contact within the sign review division who could provide a brief status update or explain typical timelines, I’d deeply appreciate it.
Thank you for the important work your team does in keeping the City of Phoenix running smoothly. I know how many requests come through your office, and I’m grateful for your time and any guidance you can offer.
Kind regards,
Alex

body:
Steve,

Thank you so much!

---------- Forwarded message ---------
From: Mina Hernandez <mina@maloufproperties.com>
Date: Wed, Oct 15, 2025 at 12:39 PM
Subject: RE: Pati's Rum Cakes Signage for building
To: Pati brannon <patibrannon@gmail.com>


Pati,



First of all, your sign person is using vinyl, not plexiglass, and the
number he is using cannot be seen on the layout that you sent to us.
Secondly, there are other changes that need to be made as well.  The
entire sign, including the Logo, must be centered above the arch.
Currently only Rum Cakes is centered over the arch.   Robert spoke to
you both early on about the sign color; he said that you walked
outside and looked at the Chiropractic sign next door which is blue.
He didn’t want too blue signs side by side, and  you all agreed that
you could use yellow.  Please have your sign person make the sign
Yellow #2016 including “Pati’s”.    Robert is ok with the height of
“Pati’s at 2’, but has indicated that the “Rum Cakes” letters should
be 1’ 6” (18” in total) as the 12” shown is too small.



I hope this will clarify things for you.



Mina



From: Pati brannon <patibrannon@gmail.com>
Sent: Wednesday, October 15, 2025 12:04 PM
To: Mina Hernandez <mina@maloufproperties.com>
Subject: Re: Pati's Rum Cakes Signage for building



We read the criteria...

and thought we have a Choice of the color, so we chose the blue so it
would all match. Please advise.



Here's your criteria below:



3. Wall signs to be individual pan channel 22 gauge metal letters,
with 1/8” acrylate

Hi Adam,

Thank you for sending the revised drawings and update. We’ve completed our internal review of the latest Dunkin’ Avondale sign package, and our Electrical & Sign Code Compliance Report is attached for your reference.  Overall, the submittal aligns with Avondale’s C-3/PAD sign standards and meets the applicable NEC and UL requirements for illuminated signage. The proposed wall sign dimensions and placements are within the allowable area and consistent with prior approvals.  However, as noted in our report:

*	The disconnect switch locations and bonding/grounding notes required by NEC 600.6(A)(1) and 600.7(A) are not currently shown on the electrical drawings. These need to be added before the next permit resubmittal.
*	All metallic sign housings, raceways, and conduits must be bonded to the equipment grounding conductor, and each illuminated sign must include a lockable disconnect switch within sight of the unit.
*	Once these items are incorporated, the package will be fully compliant and ready for city review.


Regarding the clearance bar, our understanding is that Avondale’s code restricts freestanding drive-thru accessories with moving or swing elements, which is why the clearance bar was previously disallowed. We defer to Cole for final confirmation, but a static, non-lettered clearance device may be acceptable under current code if treated as a protective structure rather than a sign.

body:
Hello Marc! Good morning. 

I received an out of the office message from Tony and was asked to reach out to you on the below.

Main thing right now really is to just get signage up on our buildings. Our building is up and bare, and we are opening soon. We can wait for the monument sign if that is the harder thing to run through the process. '

Any and all info is deeply appreciated.

Thanks!

Kind regards,
Alex

Cc: Scott Frazer <scott@christysigns.com>
Subject: Re: Hi Anthony! Checking in, and introducing myself. LPSG 251110
 
Hi Tony and Steve, 

Good morning! TGIM!

Really appreciate all the quick replies.

I am still unclear. It appears its same response that triggered my original inquiry. All I know is that the project is 'in review'. This is what Steve had let me know and he shared that he had no additional info. So, I was reaching out to get more context. I don't have any color or detail, timeline or idea of process. Kind of feels like a black hole, so just seeking to understand. That was my purpose for reaching out. Anthony: is there someone on your team that could help me walk me through where we are at and what to expect next beyond that we are just 'in review' until we are not' which is what I feel is all I have. It's sad seeing our building up with no signage.

And again, I completely understand that review times can vary and that your team is surely managing a large volume of projects. However, at this point, we’re struggling to get clarity on the status, next steps, and expected timing.
Our signage partner and our team have both been checking the system, but the only update available continues to show “in review.” We’d be grateful for any additional context or insight you could provide—such as where the project currently stands in the process, whether any feedback or revisions are pending, and what typical turnaround times are at this stage.
My goal isn’t simply to push for speed (although we are eager for signs, at minimum for the bare building) but to better understand the process and expectations so that we can plan future projects more effectively. We want to ensure we’re doing our part to avoid similar bottlenecks and that future openings don’t occur with finished buildings sitting without signage for weeks.
If there’s a contact within the sign review division who could provide a brief status update or explain typical timelines, I’d deeply appreciate it.
Thank you for the important work your team does in keeping the City of Phoenix running smoothly. I know how many requests come through your office, and I’m grateful for your time and any guidance you can offer.
Kind regards,
Alex

Our signage partner and our team have both been checking the system, but the only update available continues to show “in review.” We’d be grateful for any additional context or insight you could provide—such as where the project currently stands in the process, whether any feedback or revisions are pending, and what typical turnaround times are at this stage.
My goal isn’t simply to push for speed (although we are eager for signs, at minimum for the bare building) but to better understand the process and expectations so that we can plan future projects more effectively. We want to ensure we’re doing our part to avoid similar bottlenecks and that future openings don’t occur with finished buildings sitting without signage for weeks.
If there’s a contact within the sign review division who could provide a brief status update or explain typical timelines, I’d deeply appreciate it.
Thank you for the important work your team does in keeping the City of Phoenix running smoothly. I know how many requests come through your office, and I’m grateful for your time and any guidance you can offer.
Kind regards,
Alex
